extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners and parties (attorneys or pro se) litigating disciplinary proceedings before the USPTO (OED) and counsel preparing or opposing requests for reconsideration or motions for leave.
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for filing and opposing requests for reconsideration and motions for leave (including replies) in USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline proceedings, especially the interplay of 37 C.F.R. §11.56(c) and §11.3. Focuses on when waivers/suspensions of regulatory filing rules are appropriate and what constitutes 'new evidence' or extraordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §11.56(c) response-only framework
rubrics_metrics.description: After a request for reconsideration is filed, '[t]he other party may file a response to the request for reconsideration within 14 days of the filing of the request.' There is no allowance in the rule for a Reply brief, or any other filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests and responses under §11.56(c) are tightly constrained: the rule permits only a response within 14 days and does not provide for replies. Allowing additional filings would require use of §11.3 to suspend or waive that regulatory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §11.3 suspension/waiver standard
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In an extraordinary situation, when justice requires, any requirement of the regulations of this Part which is not a requirement of statute may be suspended or waived by the USPTO Director.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §11.3 imposes a high standard: it is reserved for extraordinary situations when justice requires. It is not intended as a mechanism to permit unlimited attempts to raise new arguments or filings that the regulations do not allow. A party seeking waiver/suspension must make the requisite showing under §11.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-situation/new-evidence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of discovery of new evidence must meet the §11.3 'extraordinary situation' threshold and cannot be merely additional arguments that could have been raised earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proponent must show the evidence could not have been discovered by reasonable diligence and that circumstances are extraordinary. Merely presenting additional arguments or newly framed claims about previously known facts is insufficient to satisfy §11.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due diligence and timing of objections
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting new evidence or extraordinary circumstances must show why the evidence could not have been discovered earlier by reasonable diligence, particularly where the party had notice of relevant events or delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to object or seek relief timely (e.g., after being aware of a delay or after formal notice such as an ALJ memorandum) weighs against a finding of due diligence and undermines claims that newly-identified matters are truly 'new evidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of arguments not raised at hearing appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that could have been raised during the hearing appeal but were not are deemed waived and generally cannot be raised later in reconsideration pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere re-presentation of additional arguments in a reconsideration request does not overcome waiver; precedent supports denying reconsideration where appellant fails to raise issues in the initial appeal and attempts later to present them as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for leave to file a reply must satisfy §11.3
rubrics_metrics.description: Because §11.56(c) does not permit a reply, any motion for leave to file a reply during reconsideration requires a proper §11.3 showing to justify suspending or waiving the regulatory prohibition on replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the movant fails to satisfy the §11.3 standard (i.e., does not demonstrate an extraordinary situation or requisite showing), the motion for leave to file a reply will be denied.
